1.pericope_label: Praise ye the Lord: he buildeth up Jerusalem, healeth the broken in heart, and telleth the number of the stars

schools.summary: Augustine will not let the goodness of praise rest in the singing, since the tongue praises but for a while and the life must praise ever, and explains that a psalm is a song to an instrument, so that the singer accompanies his voice with his hands.

Gill reads the rebuilt city as the Gospel church with Christ for its builder and the broken in heart as those whom he alone can cure, and reports the ancient astronomers who fixed the stars at a thousand and some odd before telescopes showed more; Calvin takes the psalm as untitled in the Hebrew, cites a bishop who called it a thanksgiving of the returned captives, and turns the commendation of praise into a rebuke of the common weariness at the mention of God.

Henry divides the goodness of praise into the pleasant and the comely, holding that praising God is work that is its own wages and that in giving honour to God we do ourselves a great deal of honour, and makes the stars soldiers that are mustered and marshalled; Spurgeon hears the whole book ending in a cataract of praise and prefers singing with heart and voice to singing in the heart alone.

Clarke dates the psalm after the captivity from its second and thirteenth verses, notes that every version but the Chaldee begins a new psalm at the twelfth verse so that the numbering catches up with the Hebrew, and traces the word for broken to a root from which our word shiver comes.

Keil and Delitzsch want no title at all, assigning the psalm to the restoration period and setting out the arrival of the priest with about two thousand exiles and of the cup-bearer thirteen years later; Ellicott attends to the words rather than the duty, weighing whether the poet altered a line of an earlier psalm on purpose, and glossing the outcasts from the term a prophet uses of the dispersion.

debates: Who wrote it, and when? Clarke reports the versions that give it to Haggai and Zechariah and dates it to the rebuilding after the captivity. Calvin repeats that ascription, though his English names Zephaniah where the Greek title he quotes names Zechariah, and adds a bishop who called it a thanksgiving of the returned captives and Jewish writers who refer it forward to a future rebuilding and the days of Messiah. Keil and Delitzsch drop the question of a named author and argue from tone alone that it belongs to the restoration period, filling out the history with dates and regnal years. Gill connects it instead with the psalm before it and reads the whole in the church rather than in history.
outliers: Clarke alone explains why the psalm numbering of the versions finally agrees with the Hebrew here, since all but one of them divide this psalm at the eleventh verse and so make up the one they had been running behind.

Gill answers the counting of the stars with the state of astronomy, reporting the ancient figure of a thousand and some odd and observing that the telescope has since shown more and that the clusters of the Milky Way cannot be told at all.
Ellicott is the only voice troubled by the entrance of the stars, calling the reference abruptly introduced even while granting that the train of thought is clear.
Calvin turns a verse in praise of praise into a censure, saying it condemns the all but universal sin of becoming wearied at the very mention of God.
themes: a psalm sung with the voice and with the hands
a title claimed for two prophets
the numbering of the psalms catching up
stars counted before and after the telescope
outcasts gathered by being given repentance

7.pericope_label: Sing unto the Lord with thanksgiving: he covereth the heaven with clouds, giveth to the beast his food, and delighteth not in the strength of the horse

schools.summary: Spurgeon reads the call to answer devotionally, since God speaks in his works and our lives should be responses to his love, and takes the mention of the harp as occasion to say that music was commendable under a dispensation of ritual, that those who now judge it less desirable in public worship still rejoice in it privately, and that it is a profanation for choice minstrelsy to be given to unworthy themes.

Gill explains the clouds as vapours drawn up by the sun and returned in showers before making them an emblem of afflictive providences that tend to make the saints more holy, argues from the fed beasts that God will much more feed his own people, and treats the horse militarily as a vain thing for safety however pleasing a mounted troop may look.

Clarke takes the verb as a direction to sing responsively in parts, records a half-line about herb for the service of man that five versions preserve and the Hebrew has lost, reads the horse and the legs as the two things men most admire, and holds that the preceding psalm ends at the eleventh verse in every version but the Chaldee so that these are two distinct psalms; Wesley explains that the ravens are named as the most contemptible of birds, unclean and forsaken by their dams.

Ellicott reports the literal answer and the antiphonal arrangement some infer from it, marks a fresh departure here though the strophes are only loosely defined, and calls the antithesis of horse and legs strange, preferring to explain the second clause from the standing epithet of the swift-footed Achilles; Keil and Delitzsch pass over the nature imagery and note only that the Greek makes a separate psalm of the section beginning at the twelfth verse.

debates: Is this one psalm or two? Clarke states that the preceding psalm ends at the eleventh verse in all the versions but the Chaldee, and declares his own belief that these are two distinct psalms whose subjects are not the same and which refer to different periods. Keil and Delitzsch report the same division in the Greek without endorsing it. Ellicott takes a middle way, marking a fresh departure at the seventh verse and again later, but holding that the strophic arrangement is only loosely marked throughout.
outliers: Clarke notes a half-line about herb for the service of man preserved by five ancient versions and lost from the Hebrew, and supplies the words he believes stood there.
Ellicott explains the legs of a man from Greek epic rather than from Hebrew usage, taking the standing epithet of the swift-footed Achilles as the best key to the clause.
Spurgeon uses the harp of the seventh verse to state his own position on instrumental music in worship, conceding its abuses while defending its private use.
Gill turns the fed beasts back on his readers, saying that in their fallen state his people are become like the beasts, and that they own it when grace calls them.
themes: a verb that means answer, not sing
clouds as weather and as affliction
a half-line preserved only in the versions
ravens forsaken by their own dams
one psalm or two

12.pericope_label: Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem: he hath strengthened the bars of thy gates, he maketh peace in thy borders

schools.summary: Henry sorts the singers, the inhabitants praising in their own houses and the priests and Levites in the city of their solemnities, holds that God must fortify the fortifications or the barred gates are no security, distinguishes peace in the borders from peace upon them, and observes that the land was enriched not with precious stones or spices but with the best wheat; Spurgeon adds that internal happiness is as truly the gift of God as external security, and that when God makes the walls salvation the gates must be praise.

Gill reports three Jewish authorities on the city addressed and follows the one that makes it spiritual, the Gospel church which is free and the mother of us all, reads the gates and bars as the security of that church against sin, law, Satan, the world, death and hell, and divides the peace into the outward peace of the church with her enemies, the concord of her members, and the peace of conscience that comes of believing.

Clarke reads the strengthened bars as a date, the walls still going up earlier in the psalm and here finished with the grain safely brought in, and identifies the neighbours who had ceased to trouble the city; Wesley cuts under the whole picture in a line, that their strength consisted not in walls and gates and bars but in his protection.

Ellicott glosses the verb for praise as properly meaning to stroke or soothe, thinks an allusion to the new fortifications probable while holding the expression plainly figurative of security and peace, and renders the fourteenth verse as placing peace for thy border with the fat rather than the finest of the wheat; Keil and Delitzsch give the rest of the psalm as a block of bare text without comment.

debates: Is the city of the twelfth verse the city that was rebuilt? Clarke and Ellicott both keep it historical, Clarke using the finished walls to date the psalm and Ellicott granting the allusion while calling the language figurative of security. Gill sets the literal sense aside altogether on the authority of three Jewish interpreters and reads the whole of the Gospel church. Henry and Spurgeon keep both, addressing the actual inhabitants and the actual priests while drawing the lesson for churches.
outliers: Spurgeon turns the bars of the gates against the loose thinkers of his own day, saying that modern libertines would tear down all gates and abolish all bars, but so do not we, because of the fear of the Lord.
Henry counts a growing population as a fortification, holding that the increase of a people strengthens the bars of its gates as much as anything.
Ellicott is alone in glossing the word for praise as properly to stroke or to soothe, a sense none of the others notice.
The Keil and Delitzsch block covering these verses and all that follow contains nothing but the text of the verses themselves, the only voice here to comment on none of the ground it covers.
themes: three Jewish authorities and no literal city
fortifications that need fortifying
peace in the borders and upon them
a land made glorious by wheat
a commentary block with no comment

15.pericope_label: He sendeth forth his commandment upon earth: he giveth snow like wool, he casteth forth his ice like morsels, he sheweth his word unto Jacob

schools.summary: Gill offers four candidates for the commandment that runs swiftly, the rain, the decree of God, the essential Word who came in the fulness of time, and the word of the Gospel sent out with the apostles; he collects four ancient descriptions of snow before turning it useful as a covering that keeps the wheat safe from the cold, reads the ice as hail and so as expressive of the judgments of God, and marks the nineteenth verse as the passage from nature and providence to the blessings of grace.

Clarke keeps the word personified as a very active agent running everywhere, answers the question who can stand before his cold from two crusading chroniclers who record men and beasts of burden killed by the cold of that country, and states the exclusive claim flatly, that to no nation of the world beside had God given a revelation of his will; Wesley makes the commandment sufficient without instruments and presses the hoar frost and ashes as far as their burning quality.

Ellicott takes the word as a messenger sent first to bind the earth with frost and then to release it, guesses that some extraordinary season of frost kindled the poet so that he improves on the model he is following, quotes a traveller on flakes the size of a walnut, sets the turn to Israel within the structure of the psalm, and corrects the last verse so that the judgments are not manifestations of wrath but the display of righteousness.

debates: What is the commandment that runs so swiftly? Gill lists a Jewish reading that makes it the rain, since frost and snow follow it, and another that makes it the decree of God; the Targum makes it the essential Word who came speedily in the fulness of time; and Gill himself prefers the word of the Gospel carried out by the apostles. Clarke and Ellicott both decline the question and keep the personification, Clarke calling it an active agent running everywhere and Ellicott a messenger sent out to bind the earth with frost and then to loose it.
outliers: Gill and Ellicott quote the same Latin epigram on snow as a thick fleece of waters, apparently without knowledge of each other, Gill among four ancient descriptions and Ellicott beside a traveller’s note on flakes the size of a walnut.

Clarke answers a rhetorical question about cold with two crusading chronicles, one reporting deaths on an expedition against Mount Tabor in December and the other thirty men killed in the mountains near the Dead Sea.
Ellicott alone treats the frost as biographical, suggesting that an extraordinary season of it kindled the poet and drove him to improve on the psalm he was imitating.
Wesley extends the comparison of hoar frost to ashes beyond colour and smallness of parts to its burning quality, a likeness none of the others draw.
themes: four candidates for one commandment
snow as woolly water and fleece
hail as plague and as judgment
crusaders killed by the cold
from the weather to the law
